name: Second Class
description: Second Class builds outdoor independence: Leave No Trace, fire and stove use, camp cooking, map and compass, nature observation, swimming and water rescue, more first aid, fitness, citizenship and personal safety.

provenance.notes: Topic outline drafted from maintainer familiarity with the Scouts BSA rank requirements (the structure introduced in 2016 and revised since) and cross-referenced with secondary sources found by web search. Official rank requirements could not be reached from the build environment. Some sub-requirements under 6, 8 and 9 are not yet transcribed.

references.label: Wikipedia: Ranks in Scouts BSA (secondary source)

requirements.title: Outdoor activities and ethics

children.title: Leave No Trace in practice
children.summary: Explaining the principles of Leave No Trace and how you practiced them.
children.orientation: The seven principles are: plan ahead and prepare; travel and camp on durable surfaces; dispose of waste properly; leave what you find; minimize campfire impacts; respect wildlife; be considerate of others. Being able to give a real example from your own trip for each is far more convincing than reciting the list.

children.title: Preparing fuel

children.title: Building and extinguishing a fire
children.summary: Building a fire at an approved place and time, then putting it out completely with minimal impact.
children.orientation: Before you light anything, check fire restrictions and have water and a shovel at hand. To put a fire out, the method taught by the Forest Service is to drown it with water, stir the ashes, drown it again, and feel for heat with the back of your hand. If it is too hot to touch, it is too hot to leave. Burying coals is not enough — they can keep smoldering.
children.note: Only where local fire restrictions allow and with adult supervision.

children.title: Compass and map basics
children.summary: How a compass works, orienting a map, and explaining map symbols.
children.orientation: Topographic maps show the shape of the land with contour lines: lines close together mean steep ground. Orienting the map means turning it so north on the map points north on the ground. The USGS primer covers contour lines, scale, symbols and bearings, and explains declination — the difference between true north and magnetic north.

children.orientation: Safe swimming relies on layers of protection: qualified supervision, knowing each swimmer’s ability, a buddy for everyone, and staying in designated areas. The CDC and Red Cross pages explain why swimming with a buddy matters even for strong swimmers.

children.title: First aid for serious conditions
children.summary: First aid for a list of conditions including heat and cold illnesses, shock, puncture wounds and more serious burns.
children.orientation: This step moves from minor injuries to conditions that can become serious. For heat, learn how heat exhaustion differs from heat stroke, which is a 911 emergency. For cold, learn the early signs of hypothermia — shivering, confusion, fumbling hands. For shock, learn the pale, clammy skin and weak, rapid pulse, and why you call for help immediately.

provenance.notes: Requirement numbering and topics were checked against excerpts of official Scouting America pages (scouting.org) returned by a search index on 2026-10-24. The pages themselves could not be opened from the build environment, so wording was not compared word for word and some sub-items may be summarized from partial excerpts. Summaries are ScoutPath's own words. Excerpts differed on the exact list of conditions in 6a; the summary stays general.
